overview: The atlas name Saces is a French-derived plural for Saka, but its single century-long polygon should not be mistaken for one documented Saka state. It covers much of the Tian Shan and Jetysu, including Issyk, Almaty, Bishkek, Taraz, Tashkent, and Osh. Historical texts and archaeology show a more complicated region. By 100 BCE Wusun rulers were prominent around the Ili and Issyk-Kul, while Saka, Yuezhi, and other communities had moved, mixed, or remained in overlapping landscapes. Earlier Saka burials, settlements, craft traditions, and exchange networks still illuminate inherited local lifeways, although they cannot be shifted automatically into every household of this exact century. People combined mobile herding with farming, settlements, pottery, textiles, metalwork, and long-distance connections. Evidence for family networks survives in burials and ancient DNA; evidence for formal schools, medical systems, sewers, and toilets is much thinner. The famous inscribed Issyk bowl predates this interval and its language and origin remain debated, so no secure Saka-authored writing sample is supplied. At 1 BCE the atlas layer disappears, but Saka people and practices did not collectively vanish. The ending therefore records cartographic transformation, with no invented conqueror or successor.

periods.title: 100 to 88 BCE: a mixed region at the atlas opening
periods.summary: The atlas begins its Saces layer at 100 BCE, while Han accounts place Wusun power around Ili and Issyk-Kul and remember earlier Saka movement. These sources describe diplomacy from an outside court. They do not prove that every community inside the polygon shared one ruler, name, language, or migration story.

periods.title: 88 to 76 BCE: routes, herds, and mountain basins
periods.summary: Annotated Han geography connects Wusun herding to the Ili, Naryn, Chu, and Issyk-Kul basins and places important routes across the Tian Shan. Such descriptions help locate political and pastoral worlds, but later editors and modern identifications add uncertainty. The twelve-year block is a teaching window, not a dated Saka event.

periods.title: 76 to 64 BCE: names carried by outsiders
periods.summary: Saka labels in Persian, Greek, Indian, and Chinese traditions cover related but distinct groups. Han narratives recall Sai or Saka movements southward while other communities remained or mixed. This interval keeps the atlas name visible without treating one foreign ethnonym as proof of a unified kingdom across Jetysu.

periods.title: 64 to 52 BCE: mixed Wusun and Saka communities
periods.summary: A UNESCO synthesis describes Wusun authority in Semirechye over a population that included locally absorbed Saka and Yuezhi elements. It also records combined herding and agriculture. These are regional patterns, not a census of identity, and they make the atlas label Saces especially unsuitable as a single ethnic border.

periods.title: 52 to 40 BCE: chronology from graves and settlements
periods.summary: Archaeological chronology in south-east Kazakhstan increasingly separates material phases from names supplied by classical and Chinese texts. A vessel, burial plan, or house may date activity without declaring the occupants' ethnicity. This interval therefore avoids assigning a convenient Saka king to evidence that cannot identify one.

periods.title: 40 to 28 BCE: connected pastoral and settled worlds
periods.summary: Museum chronology places Saka and related mobile groups within long-running networks of herding, political competition, towns, and exchange. Movement did not exclude settlement or farming, and portable objects could cross many communities. The evidence supports connected lifeways more securely than a neat event for these particular twelve years.

periods.title: 28 to 16 BCE: work across ecological zones
periods.summary: UNESCO's regional history shows pastoralism, agriculture, irrigation, pottery, and metalwork coexisting across northern Central Asia. Some examples lie beyond the exact polygon or begin earlier, so they establish possibilities and networks rather than a uniform Saces economy. Local valleys and water access shaped what households could actually do.

periods.title: 16 to 1 BCE: settlement landscapes outlast map labels
periods.summary: Eastern Semirechye survey joins settlements, fields, wintering places, and burial grounds into one lived landscape. Individual components have broad or uncertain dates, yet the pattern warns against making mobility and settled work opposites. The atlas removes Saces at 1 BCE without recording a matching evacuation, conquest, or cultural extinction.

sections.title: Exact identity, chronology, and the only polygon

items.text: The exact id is saces, indexed as an approximate historical-basemap record from 100 to 1 BCE. Coverage inherits the kind state and places it in the Asia queue, but no imported summary, source lead, or staged draft exists. The card preserves that id while clarifying a broad Saka-related label.

All fifty border snapshots were audited. Saces appears once, only in world-bc100, with properties from 100 to 1 BCE. It is absent at 200 BCE, 1 BCE, and every later snapshot. No duplicate, interval mismatch, lifetime violation, live card, or researched override was found.

The decoded feature is one Polygon with an outer ring and one interior hole, sixty-two positions, and a bounding box near 65.21 to 80.22 degrees east and 39.69 to 46.36 degrees north. Its geometry hashes deterministically, but precision in a file does not turn the outline into a surveyed frontier.

Issyk, Almaty, Bishkek, Taraz, Shymkent, Tashkent, and Osh test inside the polygon. Beshatyr, Ferghana, Yining, Samarkand, Bukhara, Balkh, Kashgar, Khotan, and Pazyryk test outside. Lake Issyk-Kul falls in the interior hole, a memorable reminder that display geometry is not historical jurisdiction.

At 100 BCE the exact polygon shares one encoded boundary arc with scythians-bc200 and one with kushan-empire, yet it has no detected area or representative-point ownership overlap. Shared drawing arcs document topology, not treaties. The atlas's neighboring shapes cannot appoint a ruler or write a succession agreement for us.

Saces is a French plural corresponding to Sacae or Saka, one of several ancient and modern labels for Iranian-speaking steppe groups. Persian, Greek, Indian, and Chinese classifications did not describe exactly the same population. The card uses Saka as a readable umbrella while refusing to turn terminology into a single census.

Han accounts place Wusun authority around Ili and Issyk-Kul during this century and recall earlier Sai movement. They also describe embassies, marriage diplomacy, horses, and routes. These court-centered texts are indispensable but external: they illuminate regional politics without supplying a Saka household diary or a complete map of local loyalties.

Modern archaeological chronology deliberately tests phases without assuming that every object style names an ethnic group. Burials, houses, and ceramics can show time, practice, and contact more reliably than self-identification. Calling all late Iron Age remains inside this polygon Saka would repeat the exact shortcut the evidence is meant to examine.

The exact saces record remains separate from scythians-bc200, a broader and discontinuous atlas umbrella, and from saka-kingdom, a later South Asian record beginning at 1 BCE. Similar names do not justify aliases, shared cards, or automatic succession. Each id has different geometry, dates, and historical questions.

Annotated route geography links Wusun pastoral country with Ili, Naryn, Chu, and Issyk-Kul, but modern place identifications sometimes remain debated. Directions measured from distant courts also privilege envoys and rulers. Ordinary residents enter indirectly through herds, fields, settlements, graves, and tools, which need archaeological evidence of their own.

Regional histories describe seasonal movement between ecological zones rather than endless wandering. Herds needed pasture and water, while farming and dwellings anchored some work to particular valleys. Families could move at different scales and seasons. The mixed pattern makes both the motionless farmer and the permanently mounted nomad poor universal models.

Routes across the Tian Shan connected Ili and Issyk-Kul with eastern and southern basins. Travelers faced passes, distances, and changing political authorities, so a line on a modern map was never the whole journey. Guides, animals, provisions, and local knowledge mattered even when court histories mainly remembered ambassadors.

Museum labels show clothing plaques, horse gear, vessels, textiles, and other portable objects carrying techniques and images across the steppe. Mobility helped things travel, but an imported material need not identify its owner's birthplace. Objects can change hands many times, a useful fact when a glittering buckle seems unusually well traveled.

Fine goldwork from the wider Kazakh steppe combines tiny components, animal images, and skilled assembly. Such craft reveals workshops, learning, patrons, and exchange rather than one isolated genius. Much of the best preserved evidence comes from elite graves, so spectacular objects must not make ordinary wooden, leather, or clay possessions invisible.

Central Asian chronology links mobile groups with pastoral economies, trade, and political change across wide environments. Drought, snow, and access to grazing could alter routes and herd survival, although no source gives a year-by-year Jetysu weather diary. Planning mattered; the climate declined to file its paperwork with the atlas.

Zhetysu settlement research records small dwellings, jars, pots, stone hoes, pestles, and axes alongside burial landscapes. These finds support farming and household work without proving that every Saka-labelled group lived permanently in a village. A site can document repeated occupation while leaving the residents' seasonal schedule only partly visible.

Round and other dwellings at Zhetysu sites used local earth, stone, and timber in varied plans. Architecture shows construction choices and shelter, yet walls rarely preserve the names, ages, or relationships of everyone inside. A floor plan is valuable household evidence, but it is not a complete seating chart for dinner.

Rakhat is a layered settlement south of the Issyk necropolis, with ceramics, worked bone, animal remains, and kiln evidence from more than one period. Excavators separate strata before assigning dates. The site's long life makes it informative, but also prevents every object from being dropped into this exact century without context.

Pottery impressions from southern Kazakhstan include millet and barley at sites spanning the Saka and later periods. The study locates settlement in ecological pockets near rivers and mountain-fed water. Cultivation could complement herding, but the intensity, ownership, and scheduling of fields varied and remain uncertain at many sites.

Large-scale cultivation in arid zones would require river or meltwater access, and some researchers discuss irrigation, while stressing that ancient systems remain insufficiently investigated. This card therefore distinguishes a plausible water-management need from a mapped canal network. Irrigation is not automatically drinking water, drainage, or a sewer.

sections.title: Meals, herds, textiles, pottery, and metalwork

items.text: Ceramic impressions show broomcorn millet more often than barley in the studied southern Kazakhstan assemblages. Several vessels were ordinary domestic forms rather than special burial pots. The result strengthens a mixed food picture, but grain pressed into clay records crop presence, not a complete menu, recipe, serving size, or universal preference.

Wusun-period evidence from the same broad region combines cattle raising with agriculture, querns, tools, dwellings, and domesticated animal bones. Because Saka and Wusun histories overlap here, these finds illuminate shared regional possibilities rather than a pure Saka recipe. Milk, meat, grain, and storage likely varied by household and season.

Grinding stones, hoes, storage vessels, and cooking pots make labor visible at settlement sites. Someone planted, processed, carried, cooked, repaired, and cleaned, even when texts ignore those tasks. Archaeology rarely preserves a worker's name or exact division of labor, so age and gender assignments must remain evidence-bounded.

Wool, felt, woven cloth, leather, wood, and reeds appear in museum reconstructions and surviving steppe objects. Textile making required repeated technical knowledge, while garments could carry sewn gold plaques for elite display. Preservation strongly favors some graves, so plain work clothes and routine mending are easier to overlook than gold.

Saka animal-style objects joined material choice, metalworking technique, compact form, and recognizable creatures. Their portability made them useful on clothing, weapons, and horse equipment. Scholars compare regional styles without treating every deer or feline as an ethnic passport. Art communicates, but it does not stamp a modern nationality onto its maker.

sections.title: Families, young people, status, and social ties

items.text: At Boz-Barmak in Kyrgyzstan, a fourth-to-second-century BCE burial group yielded usable genomes from nine of twelve individuals. Researchers found no first-degree relatives but identified several second- or third-degree links. The sample sits just before this atlas interval and reveals one mortuary network, not the family pattern of every community.

The Boz-Barmak males shared a Y-chromosome lineage while mitochondrial lineages varied. Researchers describe this as compatible with patrilocality and female mobility, while emphasizing the small sample. Compatibility is not proof of a universal marriage rule, and burial selection can differ from the living population whose relationships archaeologists hope to reconstruct.

The Issyk burial contained a richly dressed young person, often estimated at seventeen or eighteen, with thousands of gold ornaments, weapons, and vessels. It proves that youth could receive extraordinary elite commemoration. It does not reveal a standard childhood, coming-of-age ceremony, gender system, or wardrobe for less privileged teenagers.

Museum displays emphasize how elite graves used dress, jewelry, weapons, and animal imagery to stage rank. Women and men appear in richly furnished burials across the wider steppe, but grave presentation is not an everyday portrait. Social roles also belonged to people whose ordinary possessions decayed or were never placed underground.

Han-Wusun marriage diplomacy linked ruling houses and interstate strategy. Named princesses, envoys, heirs, and rival claimants illuminate elite family politics, not ordinary partner choice or household affection. A diplomatic marriage can change an alliance without becoming a rulebook for every Saka, Wusun, or mixed family in the region.

sections.title: Learning, language, and an honest blank writing sample

items.text: No securely documented Saka school timetable survives for this region and century. Metalworking, textile production, horse equipment, and repeated animal-style designs nevertheless required observation, practice, correction, and memory. That supports skilled learning, perhaps within households or workshops, while leaving teachers, pupil ages, formal lessons, and access unknown.

Children and newcomers had to learn routes, pasture conditions, animal handling, planting, grinding, storage, and social obligations. Settlement tools make those knowledge domains visible, but not a single educational institution. The safest picture is practical learning embedded in work, with no invented classroom, alphabet drill, graduation age, or universal curriculum.

The inscribed silver bowl from Issyk predates this card by centuries and may have traveled from Bactria. Recent scholarship places it within an Issyk-Kushan script corpus rather than accepting older confident Saka readings. Its short signs are important evidence, but they cannot securely supply this exact community's language sample.

New readings of Issyk-Kushan script continue to change sign values and linguistic interpretation. That progress is a reason for caution, not permission to invent a settled translation. The bowl's date, findspot, object movement, language, and author do not align securely enough with 100 to 1 BCE Saces for a quoted passage.

Khotanese manuscripts preserve a Saka language in Brahmi script, but surviving examples come from the southern Tarim Basin and much later centuries. The British Library catalogue is valuable precisely because it records language, script, material, and findspot. Those manuscripts cannot be moved backward to fill Jetysu's first-century BCE silence.

sections.title: Bodies, injuries, food, and limits of medicine

items.text: A review of Kazakhstan's archaeological medicine begins by stressing how little direct evidence survives. One central Kazakhstan burial dated centuries earlier than this card contained a healed complex shin fracture. Healing shows survival and perhaps assistance, but neither the treatment nor a specialized healer can be reconstructed from the bone alone.

Saka-period skull openings have been interpreted as trepanation, yet proposed purposes include treatment and postmortem ritual. Several reported holes showed no healing, so survival cannot be assumed. These examples come from central Kazakhstan and earlier broad dates; they do not establish a Jetysu medical system or a routine operation.

A bronze arrowhead lodged in one burial's shoulder blade documents lethal trauma more securely than it documents a physician. Weapons, falls, infections, childbirth, tooth pain, and animal accidents were possible hazards, but this card lists no remedy without evidence. Archaeology can identify injury while remaining silent about bedside words or attempted care.

Stable isotopes from earlier Saka-period central Kazakhstan vary widely and suggest millet entered some diets, whether locally cultivated or imported. The sample covers thirty-one people from several cemeteries, far from a universal menu. Diet affects health, but isotopes do not identify recipes, meal timing, individual preference, or a named diagnosis.

Broader isotope research across Kazakhstan finds changing use of C4 foods such as millet rather than one timeless steppe diet. Results differ by place, period, and person. That variation matters for health history, yet chemical signatures cannot tell whether a child enjoyed porridge, disliked it, or traded lunch with a cousin.

sections.title: Waste, sanitation, water, and funerary evidence

items.text: The consulted Rakhat report describes layers, ceramics, animal bone, worked material, and kiln evidence, but it does not identify a securely dated Saka latrine, sewer, or municipal waste service. Deposits show disposal and site formation without revealing every cleaning practice. Silence about toilets is an evidence limit, not proof that hygiene was ignored.

UNESCO records later irrigation canals and water-control landscapes along the Fergana and Syr Darya corridors. Such systems show the regional importance of directing water, but dates and places vary. A field canal is not automatically a sewer, household drain, or drinking-water pipe, and none is assigned wholesale to this Saces polygon.

Animal bone, broken pottery, ash, and craft debris can accumulate where people cook, work, discard, rebuild, or where later processes move material. Rakhat's stratigraphy lets excavators separate some episodes. It does not produce a weekly rubbish schedule, household ownership map, or evidence that one settlement's disposal habits governed an entire region.

The archaeology museum foregrounds Issyk's extraordinary costume, weapons, vessels, and gold. Burials preserve deliberate ceremony far better than ordinary washing, sweeping, or waste removal. This imbalance is historically meaningful: elites planned monuments that survived, while many daily sanitation actions left faint traces or none that current research can recognize.

Excavated dwelling plans help reconstruct shelter but do not securely label bathrooms. No qualifying source in this packet identifies a Saka toilet inside the exact interval and region. The honest answer is unavailable, which may be less exciting than a golden headdress but is considerably better than giving archaeology an imaginary plumbing permit.

sections.title: Achievements, endings, and lives beyond the layer

items.text: Across northern Central Asia, communities combined herding, farming, irrigation knowledge, pottery, metalwork, settlement, and exchange in locally flexible ways. Their achievement was adaptation across ecological zones, not conformity to one economic type. Mixed practice could spread risk and connect households, although this regional synthesis cannot measure each family's yearly balance.

Portable dress ornaments, horse gear, textiles, vessels, and carved or worked materials carried technical knowledge and visual ideas across long distances. Skilled makers solved problems of weight, fastening, durability, and display. The resulting art deserves admiration without reducing Saka achievement to gold or pretending every household owned museum-quality splendor.

Microbeads and complex gold assemblies reveal patient, precise work by craftspeople whose names rarely survive. Animal imagery connected bodies, clothing, horses, and status. These objects also preserve collaboration among patrons, designers, metalworkers, and wearers, reminding us that a masterpiece can be a social product rather than a solitary miracle.

Kazakhstan's national museum presents Saka archaeology as a major artistic and historical inheritance while preserving objects for new study. Modern conservation is part of the evidence story: excavation, cataloguing, and display shape what can be learned. Public fame should still leave room for uncertain dates, ordinary labor, and regional differences.

At 1 BCE the atlas removes saces and leaves the id absent at 100 CE. No exact event in the packet turns that seam into conquest or extinction, and related atlas records overlap rather than form a clean chain. Transformation with no predecessor or successor preserves the map endpoint without erasing continuing Saka histories.

ending.text: The card closes at 1 BCE because the exact saces feature disappears from the atlas, not because a securely matched conquest, migration, or extinction occurred then. By this century, Wusun political authority and mixed communities already complicate the inherited Saka label in Jetysu. Elsewhere, Saka groups and Saka-derived names continued through different polities, migrations, languages, and regional histories. The later South Asian saka-kingdom record therefore is not made an automatic successor, and the broad scythians-bc200 record is not treated as a parent card. Kushan, Wusun, Kangju, and other powers also followed overlapping chronologies rather than one simple handoff. Transformation with an empty successor list records the map's change, protects the exact id, and leaves social, artistic, economic, and linguistic continuities open to evidence instead of converting a display seam into a historical obituary.
